If new independent consumer survey data shows strong demand for marine coatings without incentives, we would revise T1 to likely and strengthen the recommendation.

If new evidence shows that marine retailers are willing to offer substantial rebates (e.g., 15% off) that drive purchase, we would shift to favoring T2 and recommend partnering with retailers for incentive‑driven sales.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence to justify Jotun investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its marine and protective coatings technology, based on publicly available information known by mid-2024.
constraints: Limited to public sources published on or before mid-2024; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify what Jotun already sells to individual buyers (if any).
Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, competitive positioning, and feasibility of reaching consumers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., residential boat owners, DIY home protection).
2) Expand into consumer markets without differentiation, offering existing coatings directly to individual buyers.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on B2B marine, protective, and industrial coatings.
4) Partner with or license the technology to consumer brands rather than selling under Jotun’s own consumer brand.
5) Target a different customer segment, such as automotive or construction, using the same marine coating technology.

T1.claim: Residential boat owners will adopt marine coatings if they perceive the product as a premium, high-performance solution that reduces biofouling and maintenance costs, and if Jotun can capture value through premium pricing and brand association with luxury boating.
T1.who_benefits: Jotun benefits by selling higher-margin marine coatings directly to DIY boat owners, leveraging its existing marine coating technology and brand reputation.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Boat owners shift from generic paints to marine coatings because they understand biofouling issues and are willing to pay for solutions that demonstrably reduce maintenance frequency and costs.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Jotun captures value by pricing marine coatings at a premium (e.g., 20% above standard decorative paints) and by selling directly through its website and retail partners, avoiding intermediaries.
assumptions: Boat owners are aware of biofouling issues and understand marine coatings' benefits.
Jotun can communicate these benefits effectively to DIY consumers.
Premium pricing is acceptable for a product marketed as a high-performance solution.
predictions: If offered a marine coating at a 20% premium, at least 15% of surveyed residential boat owners will indicate intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Purchase intent will be higher for owners who have experienced biofouling problems in the past 2 years.
T1.first_claim: Residential boat owners will adopt marine coatings if they perceive the product as a premium, high-performance solution that reduces biofouling and maintenance costs, and if Jotun can capture value through premium pricing and brand association with luxury boating.

T2.claim: Residential boat owners will adopt marine coatings if they receive incentives such as rebates, tax credits, or bundled discounts from marine retailers or boating clubs, because these reduce the effective price and increase perceived value.
T2.who_benefits: Jotun benefits by increasing volume sales through retailer partnerships and by leveraging existing distribution channels to reach DIY boat owners.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Incentives lower the effective price of marine coatings, making them more attractive compared to generic paints, especially for price-sensitive consumers who shop through intermediaries.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Jotun captures value by maintaining margin through retailer margins and by securing long-term distribution relationships, while the retailer captures value through higher turnover and brand association.
assumptions: Retailers and boating clubs are willing to offer incentives for marine coatings.
Incentives effectively lower consumer perceived price.
Jotun can supply enough volume to meet retailer demand without compromising quality.
predictions: If a marine retailer offers a 10% rebate on marine coatings, at least 10% of surveyed residential boat owners who shop at that retailer will indicate intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Purchase intent will be higher for owners who have received similar incentives in the past year.
T2.first_claim: Residential boat owners will adopt marine coatings if they receive incentives such as rebates, tax credits, or bundled discounts from marine retailers or boating clubs, because these reduce the effective price and increase perceived value.

X1.name: Marine Coating Incentive Test
X1.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with two price scenarios and two incentive scenarios.
X1.sample: 500 residential boat owners recruited via boating forums and social media, balanced by boat type (yacht, sailboat, pontoon) and region (Scandinavia, Western Europe).
X1.measure: Purchase intent measured as binary choice ("Would buy Jotun marine coating at the given price") and willingness to pay (WTP) measured as maximum price willing to pay (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 15% of participants will choose the premium price scenario (20% above standard decorative paint) without any incentive, indicating premium awareness and willingness to pay for biofouling benefits.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 10% of participants will choose the premium price scenario only when an incentive (10% rebate) is offered, indicating that incentives lower the effective price threshold for purchase.

X1.decision_rule: If the percentage choosing the premium price without incentive >= 15% AND the percentage choosing the premium price with incentive >= 10%, both conditions met, proceed with differentiated consumer proposition. If only one condition met, focus on that

final.recommendation: Conduct the proposed Marine Coating Incentive Test (or a simpler choice-based survey) to empirically measure residential boat owners’ willingness to pay for marine coatings without incentives and with incentives. If the test confirms that at least 15% choose the premium price without incentive and at least 10% choose it with incentive, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting premium marine‑
final.target_customer: Residential boat owners (yacht, sailboat, pontoon) in Scandinavia and Western Europe who currently purchase marine coatings through DIY channels.
final.value_proposition: A premium marine coating marketed as a high‑performance solution that reduces biofouling and maintenance costs, sold directly to DIY consumers via Jotun’s website and retail partners, with a price 20% above standard decorative paints.
final.next_action: Run the Marine Coating Incentive Test (500 participants, 10 weeks, €15,000) to validate purchase intent without and with incentives.
final.uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to public sources published before mid‑2024; no direct consumer survey data on marine coating demand exists. The test will resolve uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows <15% choose the premium price without incentive or <10% choose it with incentive, the case for a differentiated consumer proposition weakens and we would recommend focusing on existing B2B marine coatings or
If new independent consumer survey data shows strong demand for marine coatings without incentives, we would revise T1 to likely and strengthen the recommendation.

If new evidence shows that marine retailers are willing to offer substantial rebates (e.g., 15% off) that drive purchase, we would shift to favoring T2 and recommend partnering with retailers for incentive‑driven sales.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence to justify Jotun investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its marine and protective coatings technology, based on publicly available information known by mid-2024.
constraints: Limited to public sources published on or before mid-2024; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify what Jotun already sells to individual buyers (if any).
Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, competitive positioning, and feasibility of reaching consumers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., residential boat owners, DIY home protection).
2) Expand into consumer markets without differentiation, offering existing coatings directly to individual buyers.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on B2B marine, protective, and industrial coatings.
4) Partner with or license the technology to consumer brands rather than selling under Jotun’s own consumer brand.
5) Target a different customer segment, such as automotive or construction, using the same marine coating technology.

T1.claim: Residential boat owners will adopt marine coatings if they perceive the product as a premium, high-performance solution that reduces biofouling and maintenance costs, and if Jotun can capture value through premium pricing and brand association with luxury boating.
T1.who_benefits: Jotun benefits by selling higher-margin marine coatings directly to DIY boat owners, leveraging its existing marine coating technology and brand reputation.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Boat owners shift from generic paints to marine coatings because they understand biofouling issues and are willing to pay for solutions that demonstrably reduce maintenance frequency and costs.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Jotun captures value by pricing marine coatings at a premium (e.g., 20% above standard decorative paints) and by selling directly through its website and retail partners, avoiding intermediaries.
assumptions: Boat owners are aware of biofouling issues and understand marine coatings' benefits.
Jotun can communicate these benefits effectively to DIY consumers.
Premium pricing is acceptable for a product marketed as a high-performance solution.
predictions: If offered a marine coating at a 20% premium, at least 15% of surveyed residential boat owners will indicate intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Purchase intent will be higher for owners who have experienced biofouling problems in the past 2 years.
T1.first_claim: Residential boat owners will adopt marine coatings if they perceive the product as a premium, high-performance solution that reduces biofouling and maintenance costs, and if Jotun can capture value through premium pricing and brand association with luxury boating.

T2.claim: Residential boat owners will adopt marine coatings if they receive incentives such as rebates, tax credits, or bundled discounts from marine retailers or boating clubs, because these reduce the effective price and increase perceived value.
T2.who_benefits: Jotun benefits by increasing volume sales through retailer partnerships and by leveraging existing distribution channels to reach DIY boat owners.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Incentives lower the effective price of marine coatings, making them more attractive compared to generic paints, especially for price-sensitive consumers who shop through intermediaries.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Jotun captures value by maintaining margin through retailer margins and by securing long-term distribution relationships, while the retailer captures value through higher turnover and brand association.
assumptions: Retailers and boating clubs are willing to offer incentives for marine coatings.
Incentives effectively lower consumer perceived price.
Jotun can supply enough volume to meet retailer demand without compromising quality.
predictions: If a marine retailer offers a 10% rebate on marine coatings, at least 10% of surveyed residential boat owners who shop at that retailer will indicate intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Purchase intent will be higher for owners who have received similar incentives in the past year.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence to justify Jotun investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its marine and protective coatings technology, based on publicly available information known by mid-2024.
constraints: Limited to public sources published on or before mid-2024; no internal company data.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., residential boat owners, DIY home protection).

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Boat owners shift from generic paints to marine coatings because they understand biofouling issues and are willing to pay for solutions that demonstrably reduce maintenance frequency and costs.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Jotun captures value by pricing marine coatings at a premium (e.g., 20% above standard decorative paints) and by selling directly through its website and retail partners, avoiding intermediaries.
assumptions: Boat owners are aware of biofouling issues and understand marine coatings' benefits.
Jotun can communicate these benefits effectively to DIY consumers.
Premium pricing is acceptable for a product marketed as a high-performance solution.
predictions: If offered a marine coating at a 20% premium, at least 15% of surveyed residential boat owners will indicate intent to purchase within 12 weeks.

arguments.claim: Residential boat owners will adopt marine coatings if they perceive the product as a premium, high-performance solution that reduces biofouling and maintenance costs, and if Jotun can capture value through premium pricing and brand association with luxury boating.
arguments.who_benefits: Jotun benefits by selling higher-margin marine coatings directly to DIY boat owners, leveraging its existing marine coating technology and brand reputation.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Boat owners shift from generic paints to marine coatings because they understand biofouling issues and are willing to pay for solutions that demonstrably reduce maintenance frequency and costs.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Jotun captures value by pricing marine coatings at a premium (e.g., 20% above standard decorative paints) and by selling directly through its website and retail partners, avoiding intermediaries.
assumptions: Boat owners are aware of biofouling issues and understand marine coatings' benefits.
Jotun can communicate these benefits effectively to DIY consumers.
Premium pricing is acceptable for a product marketed as a high-performance solution.
predictions: If offered a marine coating at a 20% premium, at least 15% of surveyed residential boat owners will indicate intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Purchase intent will be higher for owners who have experienced biofouling problems in the past 2 years.

arguments.claim: Residential boat owners will adopt marine coatings if they receive incentives such as rebates, tax credits, or bundled discounts from marine retailers or boating clubs, because these reduce the effective price and increase perceived value.
arguments.who_benefits: Jotun benefits by increasing volume sales through retailer partnerships and by leveraging existing distribution channels to reach DIY boat owners.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Incentives lower the effective price of marine coatings, making them more attractive compared to generic paints, especially for price-sensitive consumers who shop through intermediaries.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Jotun captures value by maintaining margin through retailer margins and by securing long-term distribution relationships, while the retailer captures value through higher turnover and brand association.
assumptions: Retailers and boating clubs are willing to offer incentives for marine coatings.
Incentives effectively lower consumer perceived price.
Jotun can supply enough volume to meet retailer demand without compromising quality.
predictions: If a marine retailer offers a 10% rebate on marine coatings, at least 10% of surveyed residential boat owners who shop at that retailer will indicate intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Purchase intent will be higher for owners who have received similar incentives in the past year.

arguments.quote: Moreover, 14 % of the boat owners admitted to have used paints that are not allowed in the area studied and this is a problem well-known from other studies too (Swedish Transport Agency 2010 ).
arguments.does_not_show: The source does not show that residential boat owners are aware of marine coatings' biofouling benefits or that they would switch to marine coatings if they were marketed as a premium solution.

arguments.quote: Jotun Decorative supplies coatings for commercial buildings, public buildings, and homes, and serves both the professional and DIY customer directly and through a network of Jotun Multicolor Centers.
arguments.does_not_show: The source does not provide evidence that residential boat owners receive incentives such as rebates, tax credits, or bundled discounts from marine retailers or boating clubs, nor does it show that these incentives drive purchase decisions.

predictions: If a marine retailer offers a 10% rebate on marine coatings, at least 10% of surveyed residential boat owners who shop at that retailer will indicate intent to purchase within 12 weeks.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence to justify Jotun investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its marine and protective coatings technology, based on publicly available information known by mid-2024.
constraints: Limited to public sources published on or before mid-2024; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify what Jotun already sells to individual buyers (if any).
Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, competitive positioning, and feasibility of reaching consumers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., residential boat owners, DIY home protection).
2) Expand into consumer markets without differentiation, offering existing coatings directly to individual buyers.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on B2B marine, protective, and industrial coatings.
4) Partner with or license the technology to consumer brands rather than selling under Jotun’s own consumer brand.
5) Target a different customer segment, such as automotive or construction, using the same marine coating technology.

T1.claim: Residential boat owners will adopt marine coatings if they perceive the product as a premium, high-performance solution that reduces biofouling and maintenance costs, and if Jotun can capture value through premium pricing and brand association with luxury boating.
T1.who_benefits: Jotun benefits by selling higher-margin marine coatings directly to DIY boat owners, leveraging its existing marine coating technology and brand reputation.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Boat owners shift from generic paints to marine coatings because they understand biofouling issues and are willing to pay for solutions that demonstrably reduce maintenance frequency and costs.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Jotun captures value by pricing marine coatings at a premium (e.g., 20% above standard decorative paints) and by selling directly through its website and retail partners, avoiding intermediaries.
assumptions: Boat owners are aware of biofouling issues and understand marine coatings' benefits.
Jotun can communicate these benefits effectively to DIY consumers.
Premium pricing is acceptable for a product marketed as a high-performance solution.
predictions: If offered a marine coating at a 20% premium, at least 15% of surveyed residential boat owners will indicate intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Purchase intent will be higher for owners who have experienced biofouling problems in the past 2 years.
T1.first_claim: Residential boat owners will adopt marine coatings if they perceive the product as a premium, high-performance solution that reduces biofouling and maintenance costs, and if Jotun can capture value through premium pricing and brand association with luxury boating.

T2.claim: Residential boat owners will adopt marine coatings if they receive incentives such as rebates, tax credits, or bundled discounts from marine retailers or boating clubs, because these reduce the effective price and increase perceived value.
T2.who_benefits: Jotun benefits by increasing volume sales through retailer partnerships and by leveraging existing distribution channels to reach DIY boat owners.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Incentives lower the effective price of marine coatings, making them more attractive compared to generic paints, especially for price-sensitive consumers who shop through intermediaries.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Jotun captures value by maintaining margin through retailer margins and by securing long-term distribution relationships, while the retailer captures value through higher turnover and brand association.
assumptions: Retailers and boating clubs are willing to offer incentives for marine coatings.
Incentives effectively lower consumer perceived price.
Jotun can supply enough volume to meet retailer demand without compromising quality.
predictions: If a marine retailer offers a 10% rebate on marine coatings, at least 10% of surveyed residential boat owners who shop at that retailer will indicate intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Purchase intent will be higher for owners who have received similar incentives in the past year.

X1.name: Marine Coating Incentive Test
X1.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with two price scenarios and two incentive scenarios.
X1.sample: 500 residential boat owners recruited via boating forums and social media, balanced by boat type (yacht, sailboat, pontoon) and region (Scandinavia, Western Europe).
X1.measure: Purchase intent measured as binary choice ("Would buy Jotun marine coating at the given price") and willingness to pay (WTP) measured as maximum price willing to pay (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 15% of participants will choose the premium price scenario (20% above standard decorative paint) without any incentive, indicating premium awareness and willingness to pay for biofouling benefits.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 10% of participants will choose the premium price scenario only when an incentive (10% rebate) is offered, indicating that incentives lower the effective price threshold for purchase.

revisions.reason: Simulated warehouse test (SYN-D) concerns packing errors and does not address consumer willingness to pay for marine coatings, premium positioning, or incentive mechanisms. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Conduct the proposed Marine Coating Incentive Test (or a simpler choice-based survey) to empirically measure residential boat owners’ willingness to pay for marine coatings without incentives and with incentives. If the test confirms that at least 15% choose the premium price without incentive and at least 10% choose it with incentive, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting premium marine‑
final.target_customer: Residential boat owners (yacht, sailboat, pontoon) in Scandinavia and Western Europe who currently purchase marine coatings through DIY channels.
final.value_proposition: A premium marine coating positioned as a high‑performance solution that reduces biofouling and maintenance costs, sold directly to DIY consumers via Jotun’s website and retail partners, with optional incentives from retailers.
final.next_action: Run the Marine Coating Incentive Test (500 boat owners, 10 weeks, €15,000) to validate premium willingness without incentives and with incentives.
final.uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to public sources published before mid‑2024. There is no direct consumer survey data on marine coating demand, price sensitivity, or incentive preferences. The test is needed to resolve uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows <15% choose the premium price without incentive, T1 would be contradicted and the recommendation would shift to incentive‑driven pricing.
If new evidence shows strong consumer awareness of biofouling benefits and willingness to pay a premium without incentives, T1 would become likely and the recommendation would strengthen.

frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, leveraging evidence available in 1993.
constraints: Limited public information on Tanita’s existing consumer reach and sales performance in 1993.

Financial data for Tanita is not available in the dossier; any financial conclusions must be noted as unavailable.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home fitness, weight management, or medical self‑monitoring).

frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, leveraging evidence available in 1993.
constraints: Limited public information on Tanita’s existing consumer reach and sales performance in 1993.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline are analyst assumptions for evaluating alternatives.
Evidence must be from sources published on or before 1993; later developments are not usable.
Financial data for Tanita is not available in the dossier; any financial conclusions must be noted as unavailable.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home fitness, weight management, or medical self‑monitoring).
2) Expand the existing B2B proposition (clinics, health clubs) by offering the analyser as a rental or subscription service to increase market penetration.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on commercial and institutional customers, maintaining the current product and distribution model.
4) License the bioelectrical impedance technology to consumer electronics manufacturers for integration into home appliances or wearable devices.

frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, leveraging evidence available in 1993.
constraints: Limited public information on Tanita’s existing consumer reach and sales performance in 1993.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline are analyst assumptions for evaluating alternatives.
Evidence must be from sources published on or before 1993; later developments are not usable.
Financial data for Tanita is not available in the dossier; any financial conclusions must be noted as unavailable.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home fitness, weight management, or medical self‑monitoring).
2) Expand the existing B2B proposition (clinics, health clubs) by offering the analyser as a rental or subscription service to increase market penetration.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on commercial and institutional customers, maintaining the current product and distribution model.
4) License the bioelectrical impedance technology to consumer electronics manufacturers for integration into home appliances or wearable devices.

arguments.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, leveraging evidence available in 1993.
constraints: Limited public information on Tanita’s existing consumer reach and sales performance in 1993.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline are analyst assumptions for evaluating alternatives.
Evidence must be from sources published on or before 1993; later developments are not usable.
Financial data for Tanita is not available in the dossier; any financial conclusions must be noted as unavailable.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home fitness, weight management, or medical self‑monitoring).
2) Expand the existing B2B proposition (clinics, health clubs) by offering the analyser as a rental or subscription service to increase market penetration.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on commercial and institutional customers, maintaining the current product and distribution model.

frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, leveraging evidence available in 1993.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home fitness, weight management, or medical self‑monitoring).

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, using evidence available by late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, market opportunity, and ACR’s ability to reach individual buyers.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must address the specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness) and not just general consumer interest.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness) using the 406 MHz distress-beacon technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B/industrial focus without creating a consumer proposition (status quo).
3) License the 406 MHz technology to third parties for consumer applications rather than building a proprietary consumer product.
4) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on current markets (ships, aircraft, military, commercial marine).

T1.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a reliable emergency alert in remote areas where other communication methods are limited.
T1.who_benefits: Consumers engaged in high‑risk outdoor activities (e.g., hikers, climbers, mariners) who need a distress alert system that works in isolation from cell towers or radio networks.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: These users currently rely on mobile phones, radios, or other communication methods that may fail in remote locations. A distress beacon that uses the 406 MHz satellite network offers a consistent, automatic alert that can be triggered by a
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the beacons directly to consumers through outdoor retailers or online, capturing the full retail margin. The company can also offer subscription services for tracking and emergency response coordination.
assumptions: Outdoor recreation participation is growing in 2002 and will continue to increase.
Consumers are willing to invest in safety equipment that provides a clear survival advantage.
The 406 MHz frequency is reliable for distress alerts in remote areas.
predictions: If a survey of outdoor recreation participants shows >30% would purchase a 406 MHz distress beacon within 12 months, demand justifies production.
Sales of the beacon will be concentrated in regions with high outdoor activity density (e.g., mountains, coastlines).
T1.first_claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a reliable emergency alert in remote areas where other communication methods are limited.

T2.claim: Emergency preparedness authorities and search-and-rescue agencies will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a standardized, reliable distress alert that can be detected across jurisdictions and integrated into existing SAR systems.
T2.who_benefits: Government emergency management agencies, search-and-rescue teams, and coast guards that need a consistent, interoperable distress alert system to improve response times in remote or hazardous areas.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: These agencies currently rely on multiple radio frequencies and protocols that may not be compatible across borders or agencies. A standardized 406 MHz system would enable automatic detection and coordination, reducing response time and
T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the beacons to government procurement channels, emergency management contracts, and SAR agencies, capturing volume sales and potentially subscription fees for tracking and alert services.
assumptions: Emergency preparedness budgets in 2002 are allocated to upgrade distress alert systems.

arguments.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, using evidence available by late 2002.

Both conditions present the same 406 MHz distress beacon at a price of €300 and ask: "Would you purchase this beacon today?" (yes/no).

X1.measure: Purchase intent conversion rate: percentage of participants who answer "yes" to the purchase question.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher conversion among Outdoor Recreation condition (>=15% of that group).

final.target_customer: Outdoor recreation participants (hikers, campers, mountaineers) and emergency preparedness consumers (homeowners, landlords, emergency preparedness organizations) in the United States.
final.value_proposition: A 406 MHz distress beacon positioned as a safety-critical device for remote, high‑risk activities (outdoor recreation) or as a low‑cost emergency alert solution for home safety kits.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer Intent Survey (Test X1) within the 12‑week timeframe and €20,000 budget, then analyze results to decide whether to proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain because there is no direct evidence of consumer demand or purchase intent for 406 MHz beacons in 2002. The FCC rule (ACR-fr-purpose) indicates the technology is for distress alerting in remote environments,
would_change_if: If the survey shows purchase intent >=15% for Outdoor Recreation or >=15% for Emergency Preparedness, the corresponding theory would become more likely and investment could be justified.

constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure actual purchase behavior between outdoor recreation and emergency preparedness segments before committing resources.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, using evidence available by late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, market opportunity, and ACR’s ability to reach individual buyers.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must address the specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness) and not just general consumer interest.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness) using the 406 MHz distress-beacon technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B/industrial focus without creating a consumer proposition (status quo).
3) License the 406 MHz technology to third parties for consumer applications rather than building a proprietary consumer product.
4) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on current markets (ships, aircraft, military, commercial marine).

T1.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a reliable emergency alert in remote areas where other communication methods fail.
T1.who_benefits: Consumers engaged in high‑risk outdoor activities (e.g., hikers, climbers, remote boaters) who need a distress alert system that works without cellular or radio signals.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: These users currently rely on cellular phones or radio for emergency communication but face limited coverage in remote locations. A 406 MHz beacon offers a proven, satellite‑based distress alert that can be deployed without infrastructure.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the beacons directly to consumers through outdoor retailers or online, capturing premium pricing for a specialized safety product.
assumptions: Outdoor recreation participation is growing in 2002 and will continue to increase.
Consumers are willing to pay a premium for safety devices that work in remote environments.
The 406 MHz frequency is reliable for distress alerts in those environments.
predictions: If a test offers a limited number of beacons to outdoor recreation groups, adoption rates will be higher than for other consumer segments.
Surveyed users will cite remote coverage as the primary reason for purchase.
Sales will be concentrated in regions with significant outdoor recreation activity.
T1.first_claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a reliable emergency alert in remote areas where other communication methods fail.

T2.claim: Emergency preparedness consumers will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a reliable, low‑cost emergency alert solution that complies with NOAA registration requirements.
T2.who_benefits: Consumers who live in high‑risk areas (e.g., coastal, remote) and need a simple, affordable way to signal distress without relying on cellular or landline services.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: These consumers currently use expensive or unreliable methods (e.g., pagers, whistles) and face regulatory pressure to register emergency devices. A 406 MHz beacon offers a compliant, satellite‑based alert that meets the FCC’s registration
T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the beacons through mass retail or online at a low price point, capturing volume sales and recurring registration fees.
assumptions: Emergency preparedness spending is a growing consumer trend in 2002.
Consumers prioritize compliance with safety regulations.
A low‑cost distress alert is better than no alert at all.
predictions: If a test offers a limited number of beacons to emergency preparedness groups, adoption rates will be higher than for outdoor recreation groups.
Surveyed users will cite compliance and affordability as primary reasons for purchase.
Sales will be concentrated in regions with high natural disaster risk.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, or market opportunity for a new consumer product.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must consider Deere’s existing distribution network of independent dealers and its current product portfolio (farm tractors, combines, industrial equipment).
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale gardening, hobby farming, or a niche agricultural activity) using existing tractor engineering.
2) Expand into a new consumer segment without a differentiated proposition (e.g., mass‑market small tractors or consumer‑grade equipment) leveraging the existing dealer network.
3) No expansion – continue focusing on the current B2B and existing dealer model, maintaining the current product and market scope.
4) License tractor technology to third parties for consumer applications, rather than building a proprietary consumer product.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Rapid growth in homeownership and small‑scale gardening in the 1950s and early 1960s creates a market for affordable, multipurpose equipment.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere can sell a basic, entry‑level tractor through existing dealers, leveraging the existing distribution network to reach individual buyers directly.
assumptions: Homeowners are willing to invest in a single, multipurpose tool rather than multiple specialized tools.
Deere can produce a simple, reliable tractor at a price point that meets the budget of small‑scale gardeners.
Dealers will stock and promote a consumer‑grade product alongside farm equipment.
predictions: If a survey of homeowners in 1962 shows >30% would consider purchasing a lawn and garden tractor for occasional use, the demand would justify a differentiated consumer offering.
Sales of a basic 110‑model tractor would exceed 1,000 units in the first year if marketed to homeowners.

X1.name: Consumer Messaging Test: Price vs Status Messaging
X1.method: Online survey with two experimental conditions. Participants are homeowners with small gardens (screened for ownership of <2 acres). In Condition A, they see a product description emphasizing affordability, practicality, and low cost. In Condition B, they see the same description plus a statement highlighting the tractor as a modern status symbol and a lifestyle upgrade. Both versions include a price point (e.g., $1,200) and a
X1.sample: 200 participants (100 per condition) recruited via an online panel matching U.S. homeowners with small gardens. Randomly assigned to conditions.
X1.measure: Primary outcome: binary purchase intent ("Would you consider buying this tractor?" Yes/No). Secondary outcome: willingness to pay (WTP) measured on a 7-point scale (1=Would not pay at all, 7=Would pay the price shown).

prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and WTP in Condition B (status emphasis) because homeowners value a modern, lifestyle-enhancing product.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, or market opportunity for a new consumer product.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must consider Deere’s existing distribution network of independent dealers and its current product portfolio (farm tractors, combines, industrial equipment).
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale gardening, hobby farming, or a niche agricultural activity) using existing tractor engineering.
2) Expand into a new consumer segment without a differentiated proposition (e.g., mass‑market small tractors or consumer‑grade equipment) leveraging the existing dealer network.
3) No expansion – continue focusing on the current B2B and existing dealer model, maintaining the current product and market scope.
4) License tractor technology to third parties for consumer applications, rather than building a proprietary consumer product.
